name: Canadian History since World War I (effective beginning in the 2026–27 school year)
subject: Canadian and World Studies
description: This course explores social, economic, and political developments and events and their impact on the lives of different individuals, groups, and communities, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit individuals and communities, in Canada since 1914. Students will examine the role of conflict and cooperation in Canadian society, Canada’s evolving role within the global community, and the impact of various individuals, organizations, and events on identities, citizenship, and heritage in Canada. Students will develop an understanding of some of the political developments and government policies that have had a lasting impact on First Nations, Métis, and Inuit individuals and communities. They will develop their ability to apply the concepts of historical thinking and the historical inquiry process, including the interpretation and analysis of evidence, when investigating key issues and events in Canadian history since 1914.

strands.title: Canada, 1929–1945
strands.describer: By the end of this course, students will:

overall_expectations.title: Social, Economic, and Political Context
overall_expectations.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
overall_expectations.text: describe some key social, economic, and political events, trends, and developments between 1929 and 1945, and assess their impact on different groups and communities in Canada, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities (FOCUS ON: Cause and Consequence; Historical Perspective)
overall_expectations.text_html: describe some key social, economic, and political events, trends, and developments between 1929 and 1945, and assess their impact on different groups and communities in Canada, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities (FOCUS ON: Cause and Consequence; Historical Perspective)

specific_expectations.text: describe some key social changes in Canada during this period (e.g., social changes brought about by unemployment or the dustbowl during the Depression; new left- and right-wing social movements; the increasing influence of American culture; northern Indigenous people becoming more reliant on European material goods), and explain their main causes as well as their impact on different groups and communities in Canada, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities

elaborations.text:
The impact of Nazism and the Holocaust on Jewish communities in Europe:

  Nazi use of antisemitic propaganda campaigns and historic tropes to legitimize exclusion of and violence against Jews
  the boycott of Jewish businesses
  barring Jews from practicing a wide range of professions
  the removal of citizenship, the right to education, voting rights, and other civil liberties
  the Kristallnacht pogrom, in November 1938, state-sanctioned violence included destruction of Jewish homes, synagogues, and businesses, with thousands of Jews arrested and sent to concentration camps
  stigmatizing Jews with various badges, such as the yellow star or armbands
  Jews forced into ghettos, isolated from the non-Jewish population, where their access to food, proper sanitation, and appropriate medical care was severely limited and they lived under the constant threat of state-sanctioned violence
  many Jews went into hiding
  millions were deported to slave labour, concentration, and extermination camps
  government directed systematic killing of 6 million Jews

Government responses in Canada during this period:

  severe restrictions on the number of Jewish immigrants and the policy of “none is too many”
  response to the Evian Conference in 1938
  the failure to offer refuge to the passengers of the MS St. Louis in 1939; from 1933–1945, Canada admitted fewer than 5000 Jewish refugees
  Jewish male immigrants and refugees from Germany and Austria were sent to Canadian internment camps alongside Nazis and other Germans during World War II

Growth of antisemitism and racism in Canada during this period:

  restaurants, hotels, and businesses discriminated against many groups, including Jewish, Chinese, Japanese, and Black people
  some businesses posted signs such as “No Jews” or “Gentiles Only”
  real-estate contracts prohibited Jews from residing or purchasing property in some Canadian neighbourhoods
  antisemitic protests such as the Days of Shame in Montreal in 1934
  some professions excluded Jewish people
  universities limited the number of Jewish students
  founding of the anti-Jewish political party the Parti national social chrétien (National Social Christian Party) by journalist and Nazi sympathiser Adrien Arcand
  harassment of Jews by anti-immigrant and antisemitic groups such as Native Sons of Canada and “Swastika clubs”
  the riot at Christie Pits

Responses to Nazism and the Holocaust by individuals and groups in Canada:

  Jewish resistance
  Jewish and non-Jewish groups coming together to oppose racism
  formation of Montreal’s Jewish General Hospital (1934)
  Jewish men and women enlisted in the Canadian armed services
  Jewish politician Abraham Albert Heaps pressuring Prime Minister Mackenzie King to reconsider Canada’s immigration laws
  actions taken by the Canadian Jewish Congress and their executive member Saul Hayes to combat antisemitism and lobby for refugee acceptance
  the work of Dorothy Dworkin and the National Council of Jewish Women of Canada, who supported the war effort and collected clothing and other goods to send to Jewish communities in Europe
  Max Enkin and the Tailor Project, which brought in skilled tailors from the Displaced Person camps of Europe during the time that Canada was still not accepting Holocaust survivors
  Canadian Jewish community support for Jewish refugees

Impacts of antisemitism in Canada to the present day:

  the incorporation of the Young Men’s Hebrew Association in Toronto (1930) and the building of the Jewish Community Centre in Toronto (1953) in response to not being allowed to join many of the existing clubs in the city
  the need for security at Jewish institutions, including synagogues, community centres, and schools, in response to threats and vandalism

elaborations.text:
The impact of the Holodomor on the people of Ukraine:

  an act of genocide against the Ukrainian people by the Soviet Communist regime 1932–1933 in which the Ukrainian population was reduced by millions
  the Soviet policies that led to famine and then forced starvation
  collectivization of individual farms and land so that the Soviet state had control over Ukraine’s agricultural resources and grain supply
  resistance by Ukrainians to the collectivization
  Soviet dehumanization of Ukrainians
  rules of law not followed – executions, deportations, incarcerations without trials and due process, or being sent to Gulag camps with little chance of survival
  destruction of churches and arrests of priests
  The Law of Five Stalks of Grain, August 1932
  farms and land were controlled by the Soviet State
  Moscow blacklisted one-third of the villages in Ukraine for not fulfilling their food production quotas
  the removal of all foodstuffs from households
  privately-owned land, homes, and equipment were confiscated by the state
  a system of internal passports only for people from cities, introduced in December 1932, prevented the movement of starving farmers searching for food
  sealing of Ukrainian borders, January 1933
  Soviet denial of the famine and refusal of international food aid from the Red Cross and others
  Russification – suppression of the Ukrainian language and culture
  resettlement of Russians in homes that were vacated by Ukrainians who were arrested, deported, or died of starvation, August 1933
  Soviet destruction of the historical memory of the famine

  Canadian journalist Rhea Clyman’s role in alerting Canada and the world to the Holodomor famine
  disinformation in the Canadian media during the famine and after
  creation of the Ukrainian Canadian Congress, 1940
  the pioneering campaign by historian Paul Yuzyk, appointed to the Canadian Senate in 1963, for multiculturalism to be adopted as official federal policy
  the world’s second and Canada’s first monument to the Holodomor in Edmonton, 1983
  recognition of the Holodomor as genocide by Canada and Ontario, with Holodomor Memorial Day on the 4th Saturday in November

overall_expectations.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
overall_expectations.text: describe some key social, economic, and political events, trends, and developments in Canada from 1982 to the present, and assess their significance for different groups and communities in Canada, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities (FOCUS ON: Historical Significance; Continuity and Change)

overall_expectations.title: Communities, Conflict, and Cooperation
overall_expectations.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
overall_expectations.text: analyse some significant interactions within and between various communities in Canada, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities, and between Canada and the international community, from 1982 to the present, and how key issues and developments have affected these interactions (FOCUS ON: Continuity and Change; Historical Perspective)

specific_expectations.text: describe some significant ways in which Canadians have cooperated and/or come into conflict with each other since 1982 (e.g., conflict over the 1992 cod moratorium; political protests such as those against the G20 meetings in Toronto or the rise in university tuition in Quebec; strikes; racism and hate crimes; continuing legal conflict and/or political protests over Aboriginal title and land rights; the Idle No More movement; the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls; continuing tension between Quebec and the federal government; cooperation in response to natural disasters such as the 1998 ice storm or the Saguenay and/or Red River floods; cooperation among members of social reform movements), and analyse these interactions from various perspectives
